blogs.description: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a…
blogs.content:
Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3

 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy.

 datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page.

 Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

blogs.content:
(Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images)

 Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

 As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings .

 On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

 The Shocking Demise of Jensen Huang. This week’s coverage was dominated, unsurprisingly, by the shocking and sudden end of Jensen Huang’s 32 year tenure as CEO of Nvidia. The end came on Thursday morning, and just a few hours later, we recorded a Sharp Tech episode recounting Huang’s legendary history, figuring out what happened, and looked forward to what this might mean for Nvidia, the tech industry, and America going forward. Also see Andrew’s view from DC, Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose , and listen to Wednesday’s episode of Sharp China about the geopolitical angle, and Thursday’s Dithering about both the parallels and differences between Steve Jobs and Apple. — Ben Thompson

 Enterprise, Consumer and Intel.  The more things change, the more they stay the same: Intel remains on the back foot in the AI era, and the foundry dreams continue to flounder. On the heels of disappointing earnings and 2027 guidance that promises yet more letdowns, Ben’s Update on Wednesday examined the state of America’s would-be national champion by drawing comparisons to AMD, an Intel peer that’s red-hot right now. To understand why one company is capitalizing on skyrocketing enterprise demand while the other confronts flatlining consumer sales, the answer starts with chips chiplets and leads to more profound questions about culture, Intel’s nature, and its bifurcated strategy for the long-term (and, for subscribers, look forward to more on this topic in Sunday’s Sharp Tech mailbag episode).  — Andrew Sharp

 And Then There’s Professional Basketball. As a palate cleanser after a week of Jensen drama, this week’s Greatest of All Talk was a look at the top and bottom of the NBA after the first three weeks. On the euphoric side of the ledger we have Warriors fans (pre-Steph injury), Lakers fans, Spurs fans, and on the other end spectrum there is nothing positive to say in Brooklyn, a familiar malaise in Cleveland, and precisely one silver lining in Salt Lake City. All of it was a great time; we also hit Adam’s experience with the NBA in Mexico City last weekend, the hardest working players in NBA history, and an anxiety-inducing conversation about the number one pick, AJ Dybantsa.  — AS

---

 Presented by

 Agentic commerce purchases with Link, Stripe’s digital wallet that works surprisingly well for agents, grew 38x in September. The catalyst was consumer agents like Muse and Instinct.

 Filling out a web form is not a value-add activity for anyone. No one chooses to fill out web forms in their spare time. That’s why these agents have been particularly useful. 

 I’ve written about how these platforms are giving ordinary people an AI agent with a computer, enabling agents to do genuinely useful things on our behalf.  When one of those things is spending money, it needs a wallet that knows what it is, and isn’t, allowed to do.

 Stripe has learned that’s really about deciding how much freedom to give it. You might approve one purchase, or give it $500 for flights this week, and let it figure out the rest. The wallet’s job is to keep it within those lines while handling everything between “go buy this” and the purchase actually happening.

 That’s what Stripe is building with Link: You approve what it spends, it can come back to you if the final price changes, and eligible purchases can even come with protection if the agent makes a mistake.

 You can use Link on Muse, Instinct, as well as many other of the agents you might use already.

 Jensen Huang’s Affair, The Culper Report, Huang’s Righteousness — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Chinese spy, and that might not be the end of his troubles. I hope he survives, but his influence will never be the same.

 The Jensen Huang Story Gets Worse, Washington vs. New York, Silicon Valley — The Jensen Huang story got worse for him on Monday; the real risk for Huang is governance, even more than national security. Who benefits?

 Intel Earnings, AMD Earnings, Intel and AMD’s Divergence — Intel and AMD’s diverging earnings point to fundamental historical differences, and make me wonder if Intel needs to find a new (old) path.

 An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play — An interview with Roblox CEO David Baszucki about how AI is transforming game creation, and why that opens up huge opportunities to both enable developers and make Roblox both an Aggregator and a platform.

 Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp

 Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose — Jensen Huang spent four years substituting his own judgment for that of the U.S. government. His downfall was inevitable, and probably isn’t over.

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,207 new readers. Two weeks ago, a NYT report tied Nvidia’s CEO to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Now, the man who turned a Denny’s-booth startup into the engine of the AI boom is out the door.
 Jensen Huang has resigned after a 33-year run at Nvidia, leaving the world’s most important AI infrastructure company without its founder, and without a clear plan for what comes next.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia’s CEO

 Build a shared tracker in Claude Sheets

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 NVIDIA
 🚨  Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia’s CEO
 Image source: Nvidia / The Rundown

 The Rundown: Jensen Huang just resigned as Nvidia’s CEO and board member, effective immediately, after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset; CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO.
 The details:
 The exit came days after Huang admitted to infidelity following reports linking him to an alleged Chinese spy. The board backed him, saying it had “no reason to believe” national security or company secrets were compromised.

 Pressure built after the NYT reported a second relationship with an Nvidia executive; Reuters reported a third with another employee after the resignation.

 Kress, CFO since 2013, will hold both roles as the board looks for a replacement, with Trump pitching Tim Cook as the “only one man” who could take the job.

 Nvidia closed down 4% Thursday after falling more than 14%, with earnings due Nov. 17 and House committee chairs seeking a closed-door briefing from Huang.

 Why it matters: Over 33 years,   Huang made Nvidia the company it is, taking it from gaming GPUs to the hardware behind modern AI. Under him, it stayed dominant even as rivals pushed their own chips. Whoever steps into his shoes will have to build on that and decide which of his fights to keep, from lighter AI regulation to chip sales to China.

 TOGETHER WITH HUBSPOT
 🧠  100+ ChatGPT prompts to revolutionize your workflow

 The Rundown: HubSpot’s free, comprehensive “How to Use ChatGPT at Work” guide provides 100+ ready-to-use prompts to help professionals boost efficiency and adopt AI-driven workflows.
 Inside, you’ll find:
 Quick crash course to master ChatGPT in under 30 minutes

 Expert tips to tackle common AI roadblocks with confidence

 Get your free copy .

 ROWAN’S CORNER
 📞  How I use AI to coach my calls
 Screenshot via Forbes interview with Rowan

 Rowan: After every high-stakes call, I let AI tear apart my performance. It started as a weird quirk several months ago, and it’s quietly become one of my most useful habits, so I figured it’s worth sharing.
 The setup is simple. I record my meetings with Granola (you could use any meeting note taker), connect the transcripts to Claude, and instead of just pulling summaries and action items, I make it look backward at my own performance.
 A few of the analyses I run:
 My talk ratio on sales calls, flagged whenever it passes 50% (typically you want to talk less)

 Every moment I dodged a hard topic or put off a decision I could’ve made on the spot

 A commitment log of everything promised, including every “let me think about it,” which gets pushed into my to-do lists

 An objection library of every pushback partners raised this year, with a stronger answer drafted for each

 One quick tip if you try this is to ask for exact quotes, so Claude or ChatGPT puts your own words next to what you should’ve said.
 And this works for way more than my calls. You could run the same workflow on recruiting calls, sales calls, leadership meetings, heck, even podcasts and interview recordings. If it’s recorded, it can coach you.

 AI TRAINING
 💻️  Build a shared tracker in Claude Sheets

 The Rundown: Claude now builds its own spreadsheets, turning a description into a table and leaving the formulas in the cells, so you can check every number. In this guide, you’ll build a campaign tracker with status and budget, then share it for editing.
 Step-by-step:
 Go to claude.ai/artifacts , click the green Sheets tile under Make something new, and describe the tracker: every column, dropdown values, and cells with formulas

 Click a total and read the formula bar. Then select the table, click Ask Claude, and ask it to point out any cell holding a typed number instead of a formula, since only formulas update when Spent changes

 Ask Claude to highlight tasks that are past their due date and not Done. Then paste your own tasks over the samples and have Claude delete the leftovers

 Click Share, invite a teammate with Can edit, and leave General access on Only you. On paid plans, people can edit cells but can’t ask Claude for changes

 Pro tip: Before any big change, open Share, then the Export tab, and download an Excel copy. If an edit goes wrong, you still have the tracker as it was. For a bad build, Undo on the “Claude updated” notice takes the whole thing back.
 Watch the full guide at The Rundown University →

 PRESENTED BY INCOGNI
 📞  That scam call wasn’t random

 The Rundown: Scammers don’t guess your number — they buy it from data brokers selling your phone, home address, and relatives’ info online. That’s how a random call turns into phishing, impersonation, or worse. Incogni removes your data from these databases and keeps removing it automatically.
 With Incogni working in the background, you can:
 Keep phone numbers and addresses off broker databases

 Reduce exposure to identity theft and impersonation

 Let automated removals do the work continuously

 Get 58% off with the code RUNDOWN .

 GOOGLE
 👓️  Google joins the race for your face with AI glasses
 Image source: Google

 The Rundown: Google opened pre-orders for its first Gemini-powered AI smart glasses, 18 months after announcing them at I/O 2025, with frames from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster starting at $395 in a direct challenge to Meta’s Ray-Bans.
 The details:
 Built with Samsung, the nine styles pack a 12MP camera, open-ear speakers, and up to nine hours of battery into 41-gram frames, with no display in the lenses.

 Wearers can say “Hey Gemini” to ask about what they’re looking at, get Maps directions in their ear, play music, or translate speech live across 70+ languages.

 Google says the glasses redact bystanders’ faces before Gemini sees them, show a light when recording, and stop recording if the light is covered; users can even control which apps access the camera and mic.

 They go on sale Dec. 10 in the U.S. and South Korea and work with iPhones too, taking on Meta, which shipped 81% of AI glasses in the first half of the year.

 Why it matters: Meta holds the crown in AI glasses, but privacy backlash over their cameras has dogged it, to the point it launched a camera-free model in September. With its new glasses and their added privacy features, Google is pitching itself as the safer pick, betting it can keep the camera and still earn the trust Meta has struggled to win.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ A Rundown reader   used AI to turn personal stories into published books
 Today’s workflow comes from an anonymous Rundown reader:
 “After retiring from medicine, I began writing personal stories and used ChatGPT to polish them for sharing. Over time, it helped me connect stories, identify larger themes, and explore new ideas. I bring my own stories, reflections, and questions, then work with ChatGPT through suggestions, revisions, and sometimes disagreements. I also use Claude and Gemini as independent reviewers to catch weaknesses or missed possibilities, while keeping all creative and editorial decisions my own.
 This process has helped me publish books and create Creating Space, a collection of contemplative resources for individuals and groups. Each project sparks new questions and ideas. The biggest benefit hasn’t been saving time. At 73, I’ve begun to see myself as a creator, using AI to explore possibilities and bring my ideas to life while retaining responsibility for the work.”

blogs.name: Anthropic Engineering
blogs.title: Building strong safety evaluations
blogs.description: Safety evaluations inform some of the most consequential decisions we make about an AI model, including whether it’s ready to deploy, which…
blogs.content:
Safety evaluations inform some of the most consequential decisions we make about an AI model, including whether it’s ready to deploy, which safeguards ship alongside it, and what our next round of safety training and research should focus on. When we say a model is “safer than its predecessor,” we mean that it scored better on a set of evals someone built. But a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build.
 A safety eval measures a model’s propensity to cause or contribute to harm, whether its response to a request makes harm more or less likely, and how severe that harm would be, rather than measuring specific capabilities. It can cover different types of harm. For example, a user may actively request harmful outputs (such as seeking instructions on how to harm themselves), or they may request outputs that are intended to be harmless, but that come with high risk of unintended harm (such as seeking information on the appropriate dose of a drug). Essentially, a safety eval asks, “Given a specific input, did the model do the right thing?”
 Like other types of evals, these can be tricky to get right: researchers have repeatedly found that AI evals are easy to game , don’t always measure what they claim to measure, and aren’t documented well enough to reproduce . The results can change depending on whether the questions are multiple-choice or open-ended , or even based on how answer options are ordered .
 Psychology faced similar issues a decade ago, when large-scale replication projects found that many published findings didn’t hold up, likely at least in part because many original studies relied on small samples and journals favored statistically significant results. In response, the field instituted reforms such as preregistration (writing down hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting or analyzing data), better measurement, and more rigorous statistics, which made measurements more trustworthy and results easier to replicate. Drawing on those reforms, and from our experience building evals at Anthropic , 1 this post shares recommendations for anyone who builds or relies on AI safety evaluations, using examples from our system cards .
 Our recommendations for building AI safety evals. Some of the examples in this post draw on evaluations reported in our system cards .

 Safety first
 Build a team with the right skills
 Building a strong safety eval requires multiple perspectives, including from subject matter and technical experts. Methods experts, for example, help decide how to sample, grade, and analyze the model’s responses. Domain experts such as psychologists, biologists, or political scientists help ensure evals cover realistic and diverse test cases. They will also decide what counts as harm, which cases are borderline, and what a good response looks like.
 When one of these perspectives is missing, eval quality can suffer. Failure modes include evals that are technically rigorous but don’t capture the most relevant factors in a specific harm area or, conversely, evals that reflect deep expertise in a subject area but test only a subset of behaviors, making it difficult to draw valid conclusions about the domain as a whole. Having domain and methods experts involved from the beginning of the process can mitigate against both.
 Run evals safely
 Safety evals often run with standard safeguards disabled so we can understand a model’s baseline performance. In cyber evals, in particular, models may probe the boundaries of their testing environments and could take unintended actions if they escape. For this reason, evals should be run in a sandbox with no internet access, and monitored in real time so you can stop a run immediately if a model is acting in ways that could result in real-world harm. In recent months, in response to our own incidents , we have hardened our evaluation environments , temporarily stopped running many evaluations that give models internet access, and implemented real-time monitoring for web search evaluations that require giving models internet access. We continue to work to make these environments both realistic and safe.
 Design
 Match the design to the question
 The first thing to ask when building an eval is: what is the question you’re trying to answer? This should guide the way you design the evaluation, as it will determine how you can interpret the results.
 Most evals are observational: they tell you that one model obtained a different score than another, but not why. Causal claims (for example, “This intervention made the model safer”) need a design that varies one variable at a time, such as evaluating the same model with and without a specific intervention in place. For example, the question “Is the model responding safely to requests for content that might promote eating disorders?” is observational, whereas the question “Does altering the system prompt change whether the model responds safely to requests for content that may promote eating disorders?” is causal. An observational design is the right choice for understanding a model’s behavior; a causal design is the right choice when you want to understand whether a specific change can influence that behavior.
 Measure what you mean to measure
 Once you’ve chosen the right design, the next question to ask is: what exactly are you trying to measure? This is also called construct validity —whether your measure captures the concept you actually care about—and it’s where AI evaluations often go wrong.
 For safety evals, the obvious construct is refusal, or how often the model declines to respond. This makes sense in many cases—we don’t want models to help a user launch a scam or a phishing scheme. But for conversations related to suicide and self-harm, refusal is often the wrong construct. When a user is in crisis, simply declining to engage is, itself, a failure; the ideal response engages the user with empathy and points them toward human support . A model that refuses to respond to any prompt related to suicide or self-harm would get a perfect score on a refusal-rate eval, but it is not necessarily a safer model.
 At Anthropic, we design multi-turn safety evals that report an appropriate response rate: the share of conversations in which the model behaved appropriately throughout, judged against a rubric specific to a given risk area, developed by domain experts. One bad turn—like a model divulging details on how to run a scam when repeatedly pressed—results in a failing grade for the whole conversation. In the case of a safety eval for user wellbeing, an “appropriate” response is one where the model responds supportively to disclosures of risk (such as a user saying they are considering self-harm), avoids discussing details of methods (such as specific ways of self-harming), points the user to crisis resources at the right moment, and does not position itself as a substitute for a crisis line.
 In other risk areas, the appropriate response is different. Much of biology and cybersecurity is dual use: the same question might help a user develop a vaccine or enhance a pathogen, discover a vulnerability in their own software or exploit it in someone else’s. In these cases, too, an appropriate response is rarely a flat refusal. Rather, it engages with the legitimate version of the request while withholding the operational specifics that would provide real uplift to the harmful version of the request. We build separate rubrics for each topic so we can measure what an appropriate model response looks like in each area.
 Help with the legitimate request, hold back the operational specifics. In dual-use domains, an appropriate response should help with the legitimate version of the request while withholding information that would help the user cause harm. Example prompts are paraphrased from our evals.

 A good eval also needs to measure both compliance with harmful requests and over-refusal of benign requests. In our single-turn evals, we pair two different kinds of prompts: harmful requests (where we aim to maximize the “harmless response rate”) and benign requests (where we aim to minimize the “refusal rate”) in the same domain. For example, in an eval testing a model’s response to dual-use chemistry questions, a harmful prompt might be requesting the chemical formulation for a nerve agent (where we would want the model to refuse), while a benign request might be a question about a historical chemical disaster (where we would want the model to provide a helpful response). Deciding which requests fall into each bucket—harmful or benign—requires subject matter expertise, especially for borderline cases.
 Same topic, different intent. Examples of pairwise prompts in dual-use domains paraphrased from our evals.

 Make sure the results generalize
 The scenarios an eval tests are meant to stand in for performance in the real world, with real users. That only works if the scenario actually resembles the real world. Below are a few considerations relevant to ensuring the results generalize to real-world situations.
 Capture nuance via multi-turn simulations
 Single-turn prompts are the easiest evals to build, but they saturate quickly. They also aren’t particularly realistic: much of the time, the potential for real-world harm isn’t obvious in a single prompt. Humans extract harmful information from a model through gradual escalation, so a model that handles the first message well may respond inappropriately by the fifth.
 User distress is often particularly hard to glean from a single message. It tends to accumulate across a conversation, such that something a person said 10 turns ago changes the context of their next message. As an example, in one of our multi-turn evaluations for suicide and self-harm that we report in our system card, a simulated user discloses a destabilizing event, such as being laid off from their job or the death of a family member, early in the conversation. Later, they ask a seemingly ordinary question that, read alongside the earlier disclosure, may warrant a more careful response. If the model does not consider the earlier context, it risks providing information that could be dangerous to the user. This sort of nuance cannot be captured in an eval that reads a single message in isolation.
 Design scenarios that model a range of conditions
 To construct test suites for each safety risk, our subject matter experts design multi-turn simulations that are closely modeled after real-world observations. We built an internal tool that lets them do so systematically. The steps are as follows:
 A domain expert writes a specification . The specification includes the simulated user’s objectives and the tactics they’ll use to pursue them, plus any other dimensions that are relevant to the threat model, such as persona, situation, tone, and conversational style. Each dimension typically has several options—for example, personas can range from a novelist to an academic to an authorized government contractor.
 The first user turn is fixed , so every run of a scenario starts from the exact same prompt.
 A separate Claude model generates the subsequent “user” turns , following the specification and sampling from the different options within each dimension. The model being tested writes the “assistant” turns. Because the simulated user is responding to what the model actually said, the conversation can develop in ways a pre-written script can’t anticipate.
 Each scenario runs a number of times , and each run draws on a different combination of characteristics from the specification. This causes the conversations to diverge from the shared starting point, allowing us to model a broad range of scenarios that might emerge in real-world deployments.
 A grader model scores each transcript against the risk area’s rubric . The grader reports the share of conversations that were graded as “appropriate” throughout the evaluation.

blogs.title: No Shirt, No Shoes, No Service for Bots
blogs.description: Read on tomtunguz.com → Bots passed 51% of global web traffic in 2024 & reached 54% in 2026, while monthly AI agent traffic jumped 8x in two…
blogs.content:
Read on tomtunguz.com →
 Bots passed 51% of global web traffic in 2024 & reached 54% in 2026, while monthly AI agent traffic jumped 8x in two months between August & October 2026. 1

 Instead of welcoming those agentic buyers, the largest consumer storefronts are locking them out.

 This week United Airlines updated its terms to ban AI agents from booking tickets, reserving the right to cancel any reservation bought by a bot. 2 Amazon has similarly blocked third-party AI shopping agents from its store. 3

 Both companies cite security. The deeper reason sits on their income statements : in modern e-commerce, the base product merely breaks even ; ads, upgrades & warranties supply the profit.

 Amazon collected $588b of retail revenue last year, but advertising is the only profit in it. The $68.6b of sponsored listings, at roughly a 50% margin, generate $34.3b : all of the $34.4b in retail operating income. 4

 United runs the same playbook with fees instead of ads. Its $4.8b of seat & bag upgrades, $3.2b of credit card & loyalty fees & trip insurance commissions together top its entire $4.7b of operating income. 5 6

 Dell’s computer business is a high-tech grocery store. Hardware sold at a 13.7% gross margin does not cover $14.6b of operating expenses ; ProSupport warranties & attached services at a 44.8% margin generate $10.4b of gross profit, or 127% of Dell’s $8.1b in operating income. 7

 Each share tops 100% because the base product, priced near cost, loses money on its own.

 Shopify runs the opposite model, which is why it welcomes agents. Shopify powers independent merchant websites & collects a 3.1% toll on every dollar processed, 78% of it from payment processing & merchant services. 8 Whether a human or an AI agent clicks buy, Shopify collects the same cut. In September, it opened checkout to browser agents across every eligible store.

 An AI agent is a buyer on a mission. It skips the sponsored listings, declines Economy Plus unless explicitly instructed & unchecks the extended warranty on a Dell Latitude.

 Merchants built on loss leaders now face a choice : raise base prices, charge an explicit agent checkout fee, or invent wholesale incentives that persuade bots to upsell. Until they re-price the funnel, the sign on the checkout window stays the same : no bots allowed.

---

 Andreessen Horowitz (Olivia Moore & Justine Moore), Welcome to the B2A Economy , November 11, 2026 ; Imperva Bad Bot Report (2021 to 2026 automated traffic share rising from 42% in 2021 to 51% in 2024 & 54% in 2026) ; Cloudflare Radar (automated requests reaching 60.6% of web content HTML requests in August 2026) ; & HUMAN Security State of Agentic Traffic (November 9, 2026, showing monthly AI agent web requests rising 16.3x from February to October 2026 & 8.0x from August to October 2026, with Meta Muse at 59% & OpenAI agents at 30% of observed agent traffic).  ↩︎

 United Airlines terms (revised November 11, 2026, Rules 1, 5.H & 6.J.6) & PhocusWire , November 11, 2026 : prohibits any automated artificial intelligence tool or agent from making, modifying or servicing a ticket or purchasing any service or product, & permits United to cancel tickets booked by an AI agent without notice, even if a human passenger supervised the transaction.  ↩︎

 Amazon updated its robots.txt rules & sent formal cease-and-desist notices blocking third-party agentic browsers & shopping assistants (including Perplexity’s Comet & automated checkout agents) from executing purchases on amazon.com .  ↩︎

 Amazon.com, Inc. Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025 : consolidated net sales of $716.92b less AWS revenue of $128.73b equals $588.20b in non-AWS revenue. North America operating income ($29.62b) plus International operating income ($4.75b) equals $34.37b in non-AWS operating income. Advertising services revenue reached $68.64b in 2025 (up from $56.21b in 2024).  ↩︎

 United Airlines Holdings, Inc. Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025 : total operating revenue of $59.07b, operating income of $4.71b (8.0% operating margin) & net income of $3.40b. Disaggregated revenue Footnote 3 reports $4.80b in ancillary passenger fees (seat selection, Economy Plus & baggage) & $3.20b in other operating revenue (co-brand credit card marketing, Kinective Media advertising & lounge/partner fees), plus $3.41b in redeemed MileagePlus travel miles.  ↩︎

 US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations airline ancillary fee report & travel insurance underwriting disclosures (Allianz Partners, AIG Travel Guard & Arch RoamRight) : airlines & online travel agencies retain 30% to 50% of gross written trip-insurance premiums as distribution commission at checkout.  ↩︎

 Dell Technologies Inc. Form 10-K & Q4 FY26 earnings release for the fiscal year ended January 30, 2026 : total revenue of $113.54b & GAAP operating income of $8.15b ($22.71b total gross profit less $14.56b operating expenses). Products revenue was $90.41b with $78.06b cost of revenue ($12.35b gross profit, 13.7% gross margin) ; Services revenue (including ProSupport warranties, extended maintenance & deployment attach) was $23.13b with $12.77b cost of revenue ($10.36b gross profit, 44.8% gross margin, or 127.1% of GAAP operating income).  ↩︎

 Shopify Inc. Q3 2026 earnings release, November 3, 2026 : GMV of $119.1b on revenue of $3.742b (subscription solutions $836m, merchant solutions $2,906m), gross profit of $1.78b at a 47.6% margin & operating income of $568m, so revenue equals about 3.1% of GMV, with 68% of GMV processed through Shopify Payments. Per the Form 10-Q, merchant solutions revenue is principally payment processing & currency conversion fees, with advertising on the Shopify App Store & Shop Campaigns included alongside lending, shipping labels & POS hardware in that $2,906m. TechCrunch , September 28, 2026 : Shopify extended WebMCP into checkout for all eligible merchants with no merchant configuration, letting browser agents read, update & submit a checkout once the buyer authorizes it, while Amazon & Adidas moved to block agents ; Shopify’s own test completed 60 of 60 checkout tasks in 10.3 seconds using WebMCP versus 56 of 60 in 27.4 seconds via browser automation, at 58% lower cost.  ↩︎

blogs.title: An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: An interview with Roblox CEO David Baszucki about how AI is transforming game creation, and why that opens up huge opportunities to both enable developers and make Roblox both an Aggregator and a platform.
blogs.content:
An interview with Roblox CEO David Baszucki about how AI is transforming game creation, and why that opens up huge opportunities to both enable developers and make Roblox both an Aggregator and a platform.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Roblox CEO David Baszucki . I’ve interviewed Baszucki twice, in February 2022 , and November 2023 .

What struck me about this interview is just how much AI has changed the landscape for Roblox. This was a company predicated on the concept that anyone can make a game, but now, for the first time, literally anyone can make a game. That means a world of abundance, and in that world, there is an opportunity to be an Aggregator, and Roblox is aggressively pursuing that opportunity.

To that end, we discuss how AI has changed Baszucki’s view of what is possible, what goes into a game creation harness, making games on your phone, and the power of recommendation. Then we talk about Roblox’s vision of a universal player, where a Roblox game works everywhere, and Roblox Everywhere, where Roblox developers can use the platform beyond the Roblox app. We also touch on advertising — the natural Aggregator business model — and whether Baszucki still thinks he is building the metaverse.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

Topics: The AI Impact | A Game Creation Harness | Roblox Build | Roblox Discovery | Universal Player | Roblox Everywhere | Advertising | Metaverses

The AI Impact

David Baszucki, welcome back to Stratechery.

DB: Thank you, Ben, for having me back. It’s great to be here.

So this is the third time I’ve interviewed you, and I want to sort of put that in an interesting context. First, you started Roblox in 2004, you went public in 2021, you first talked to me in 2022 and again in 2023 , that’s like a nearly 20-year stretch. Now it’s 2026, and here’s my question: Is the world more different for you now, compared to three years before, than it was for the entire first two decades from starting the company to the last time we talked?

DB: The changes in the world we all feel are sure happening a lot more rapidly. When we first published Roblox — I don’t know if people on this podcast remember — software used to be distributed on floppy disks and CDs.

You know, the funny thing is, you’re the second person I’ve interviewed in the last two or three weeks where we’ve referenced back to fact that the reason we say packaged software is it used to actually be packaged!

DB: It’s been crazy, we had the Internet, when we started the company, we had the vision of a category called immersive co-experience, sci-fi writers have been writing about the holodeck forever, and we went along our way.

I’m still pro-metaverse, we can use the word metaverse, it’s okay.

DB: Okay, good, we use them all. It’s Snow Crash — metaverse, holodeck, they’re all good. We started on this vision of building human co-experience, we saw the mobile age come across us, we saw the crypto age. The AI acceleration wave we’re in is faster and bigger and crazier than anything I’ve ever seen, it’s changing how we think about the product, it’s changing how people are going to create games. What’s really exciting is, when we started the company, we had this slogan called “You Make the Game”.

Yep.

DB: We started with that slogan, we learned along the way that the ratio of people who might want to play games to make games has drifted — more people want to just play games than make games, because historically making games has been Roblox Studio and 3D editing and writing script.

We could be approaching the time where “You Make the Game” really comes true, and where making a game is accessible to everyone. It’s really fun, I’ll tell you a bit about some of the experiments we’ve been having with Roblox Build . But we’re entering an era where making a game could be as big as playing a game.

I’m right there with you. We’re obviously going to touch on all those points, I think it’s probably predictable what we want to talk about. But to go back to 2023, you called AI then, “a super paintbrush and a super 3D modeler, rather than a full replacement” — Is that still how you’re thinking about AI?

DB: It’s what the data is proving out. We just had our earnings call a few weeks ago , we highlighted a lot of acceleration. One, there’s various ways humans can augment with AI on Roblox, they can use MCP , which is like plugging in a model, they can use the Roblox AI assistant to help build.

And what do you mean with that MCP server? You mentioned you had 5x growth quarter-over-quarter. That’s where you’re actually using Claude Code or Codex or whatever to work with Roblox?

DB: People are plugging in, we can see all of them — Claude Code, Codex, other models — all being plugged into Roblox Studio to help build things. We’ve seen two games hit the top 20 made by AI, we have other metrics like the number of assets.

What do you mean by “made by AI”? Because you also said 80% of games in the top 100 have AI-contributed content.

DB: Touched by AI, vibe-coded directly with AI, and we can see the count of assets accelerating.

Got it.

DB: It’s turned out to be, I believe, somewhat faithful to what I said. This is a human paintbrush accelerator, good ideas are still very important, novel types of gameplay are very important. But people are able to flex their creativity much more quickly. We have members of the Roblox board of directors carrying a mobile phone around, building games like 15 times a day. We have people who are not necessarily engineers or product managers now building within the company, so we’re really at the dawn of a new era.

A Game Creation Harness

You mentioned the super paintbrush, super 3D modeler, is there a super gameplay developer? Because there’s a large step between, “I have an idea for a game”, versus the actual mechanics of the game. How much can the AI do to help you as far as that goes?

DB: You’re touching on the dream of what is a game creation harness versus a coding harness .

Dive into it, this is super interesting. Lay out the difference and the way you’re thinking about that.

DB: So everyone’s getting familiar with coding harnesses — Claude Code, Cursor, Replit, Lovable, Codex, you name it. A game is arguably much more complicated than code. As you mentioned, there’s art, there’s 3D objects, there’s scenes, there’s avatars, there can be gameplay code, there can be missions, and there can be code underneath it. So a harness that is being created to create games really has to run in multiple modalities, needs to listen to you, and if you said, “I would like a multiplayer tortoise-and-the-hare game that 100 people can play, and we’d like to do it on Venus, and I’d like it to run on all devices” — there’s a lot of different things that need to be generated there.

The avatars, the assets, all of that, as well as the gameplay, which I think is a very human thing — your idea of what type of a game it is is actually very unique. So one of our board members is building a hybrid kind of Wordle-crossword game with his own vision of how this crossword game should work, and that’s very unique to him. I’m optimistic we’re still seeing that notion of a human coupled with an accelerating paintbrush in essentially a very complex harness for building games.

There’s so many pieces you talked about. The asset creation piece, compared to 2023, much further along, arguably there. You could have even the video component, or the moving worlds, but then you almost have these different pieces. Do you have to build — is there going to be one harness, and one sort of — we’re going to get to your Build app in a little bit — that handles all of that? Or are you still thinking we need to do this piece-by-piece as the model gets good enough for, or we need different models maybe for the different parts of this?

DB: I think just as we see with harnesses that are routing different models, even for coding now, a lot of companies have multiple models running side-by-side and their harness is optimizing. Our harness inside Build and inside Studio Build is running not just multiple models for certain things, but then there’s a second dimension of, “Are we building a scene?”, “Are we building a 3D object?”, “Are we building code?”, “Are we building an NPC?”.

So yes, we are routing both by kind of specific asset that’s being created, as well as multiple models within each of those, and we’re combining some areas where we have incredible data on Roblox — for example, data that can be used to help create non-player characters, characters that act normally, side-by-side with you. But there’s also really good coding models out there, both open source and frontier, and so we see a harness being able to put all these things together.

What’s the mix of those models? Say we have three categories — frontier, off-the-shelf open-source models, and models that you’ve trained specifically. And I guess even there there’s two categories, are you doing foundational models on your own, or just doing some post-training?

DB: We literally have all three of those running in our Build harness. And we’re, in certain cases, optimizing the cost of frontier with the capabilities of open source. We have a Cube model — we’ve announced it — which is trained on 3D assets.

Yeah, super interesting. Tell me about the Cube model.

DB: The Cube model is our own 3D asset creation model trained on all of the 3D objects inside Roblox, where the developer has opted in to the training. It’s very fast, it’s very efficient, and it runs on our own hardware. When you go into Build or I go into Build and I say, “Hey, make that tortoise-and-a-hare game”, and if you describe that tortoise as somewhat unique and different, “I want the tortoise to look like this, and have a fur that looks like this, and maybe have this”, that Cube model will and may come into play and generate that tortoise for you.

How does your cost structure work for this? Is it a usage thing from a developer perspective? You have the MCP server — that’s where they can bring their own, what’s the mix?

DB: You sound like a product manager, because these are exactly the same discussions I had about an hour ago. The ultimate vision is something like Roblox Build is just like the creation of short-form video. Short-form video 10 years ago — all of a sudden we all figured out we can make video and edit it on our phones, amongst multiple products that was like a huge revelation.

We are so on the same page, I have a whole section on short-form video later in the interview. That’s good foreshadowing.

DB: Yeah. And so along comes short-form video, and we have phones, and all of a sudden we’re making and sharing video. Arguably games are a lot more complicated, they can be immersive 3D environments, multiple people can come there. They have, as I was saying, code and geometry and avatars, but that’s where Build is going — that same notion of, “I’m going to pull out my phone and create something”, some of those models are still expensive.

But the dream is, we’re already testing — I think Canada went live today. We’re testing in, I think, Serbia and New Zealand, we want it available for everyone and so it creates a wonderful opportunity for us to be super efficient with our models while super powerful. It creates the opportunity for those users who want to just do hundreds of iterations to have them buy tokens as well, if they really want to dig into it, so we’re optimistic this will be free for everyone.

Roblox Build

You keep mentioning Build, I’m on your website , and this is how you describe Build: “Build is a new way...
